item.title: ByteDance Researchers Open-Sources Laminar, an Async Reinforcement Learning RL Post-Training Framework
item.abstract: Researchers from The University of Hong Kong and ByteDance Seed have open-sourced Laminar . Laminar is an reinforcement learning RL post-training framework for LLMs and long-horizon agents. The core idea is simple: stop forcing every trajectory and every GPU to wait for the slowest one. For teams training coding agents with long, skewed rollouts, that is where most GPU time goes. Laminar is an asynchronous RL post-training framework that decouples rollout, buffering, training and weight transfer into independent loops. It is built on verl and Uni-Agent and released under Apache-2.0. The launch blog splits the stack into 3 layers. verl provides training and inference compute backends. Uni-Agent handles agent execution, tool calls and sandboxes. Laminar handles cluster-scale orchestration. The design rests on 3 principles: full decoupling, fine-grained asynchrony and fault tolerance. In the research paper , relays are CPU processes, 1 per rollout machine. They broadcast weights along a pipelined RDMA chain. A 72B model reaches 127 other relays in under 1.6 seconds. Most async systems use version-mixed partial rollout. They interrupt in-flight trajectories at each weight update and resume under the new policy. That forces repeated re-prefill. Laminar also supports a version-consistent mode. Each trajectory finishes under 1 policy version. Replicas update independently, without a global weight-switch barrier. The blog states that this keeps the prefix KV cache intact. It argues re-prefill cost scales cubically with sequence length under frequent updates. Repack handles the tail. Once new weights exist, leftover old-version trajectories are consolidated onto fewer replicas. Drained replicas then load the new version immediately. The research team trained Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct on SWE-rebench. They evaluated on all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks with greedy decoding. Faults stay local. If a rollout replica fails, the router fences only that replica. It restarts, reloads weights from the local relay and resumes from its generated token prefix. A replica that fails during weight loading recovers without blocking the trainer. Trainer checkpoints align model state, prompt cursors and published weight versions. laminar.eval also evaluates several checkpoints at once across resident replicas, in batch or streaming mode during training. Check out the Paper , arXiv preprint , GitHub Repo and Technical Blog . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: [AINews] Math Proofs Are Landing Faster Than We Can Read Them
item.abstract: Scott Aaronson was still trying to digest two proofs of VP ≠ VNP at dinner. Before dessert, an OpenAI paper claimed that the square matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4 . During dessert, another paper claimed matching upper and lower bounds for the finite Fourier transform . The lower bound is the biggest news. In October, OpenAI found an upper bound for ω down to at most 9/4 . Finding the lower bound = upper bound leaves only one possible value, which is a shocking result for most. We plotted 64 selected AI-assisted research advances so far this year. November accounts for 20, including six preprints from Google’s Cogentic . The curve follows public releases, including proofs still under review. We count the two VP ≠ VNP proofs once and give October’s faster matrix multiplication algorithm and November’s matching lower bound an entry each. The big releases underline how much a paper count can hide. OpenAI’s catalogue lists 730 manuscripts across 375 result families, including follow-ups and companion arguments. Its revision log also records three October withdrawals after a sign error in one paper affected two others. Yupan Liu showed that two messages suffice for quantum interactive proofs , a result that would have been a big deal on its own. Aaronson says Liu used AI and that he had to remind himself the result had even happened. In other big news, today’s guest Thariq Shihipar announced his big move from Anthropic to OpenAI , the second high profile Ant→OAI move in recent times after Cat Wu . We dive into his two philosophies of AI and how and where /humans add taste. AI News for 11/25/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI-Generated Math Results: Matmul Exponent, Factoring and Lean Proofs Matrix multiplication exponent : OpenAI's model claims a lower bound matching its October upper bound, making ω exactly 9/4. Previously no nontrivial lower bound was known ( @SebastienBubeck ; repo ). Mechanism : The result reportedly comes through an explicit superlinear circuit lower bound ( @wjmzbmr1 ). Implications : Bubeck notes that a prior Lee et al. result implies LPs solvable in n^{9/4}. He also says LPs can now be solved in strongly polynomial time, a Smale problem ( follow-up ). Expert reaction : Omri Weinstein calls it "truly surreal" if correct, since most experts expected ω = 2 ( @WeinsteinOmri ). OpenAI batch : Nine new papers with Lean proofs came out a day after a claimed VP ≠ VNP proof ( summary ). Other claims : Fourier transform complexity of n√log n ( @lreyzin ). Integer multiplication : Also n√log n, tight under weak ETH ( @cloneofsimo ). Same-day solutions : Anthropic posted its own VP ≠ VNP solution the same day ( @vitaliychiley ). Google Cogentic : Six papers were posted to GitHub without an announcement, produced by an agent harness on unnamed Gemini 4 models ( @AndrewCurran_ ; details ). Results : A proven NFS-class factoring bound, beating a 1992 record. Also claimed: Deterministic subexponential factoring. Faster small-characteristic discrete log. Progress below the square-root barrier on log-rank. Edge reconstruction for linear-density graphs. Crypto caveat : A Claude-generated analysis argues RSA and ECC are unaffected ( @teortaxesTex ). Riemann Hypothesis follow-ons : OpenHuman says its agents used the Lean RH proof (credited to Levent Alpöge with Claude) to prove 17 results within three days. These include Lindelöf and Erdős #985 ( @ladyxtel ). Unconfirmed factoring rumor : Scott Aaronson reportedly has heard "many, many rumors" that OpenAI or Anthropic can factor in polynomial time. This is unverified ( @kimmonismus ). Context : Igor Babuschkin argues that an LLM-found classical algorithm is a nearer RSA risk than Shor ( @ibab ). Frontier Model Competition: Gemini 4 Neon, Fable 5.2, GPT-6.2 Astra Gemini 4 Neon momentum : Usage is surging across platforms. Perplexity usage : Neon used 44.5B tokens on Tuesday with hours remaining, 23.5% above all of Monday ( @AravSrinivas ). Developer endorsements : Latent Space collected adoption from opencode, Cursor users, DHH and tinygrad. It cites #3 on FrontierSWE at 62.4% and a Day-1 paid-API usage record ( roundup ). Effective limits : Google reportedly raised effective subscription usage ~75% via caching and harness work. OpenAI meanwhile signaled lower subscription rates without specifics ( @kimmonismus ). Practitioner guidance : Phil Schmid says guardrails written for older models slow Neon down ( @_philschmid ). Claude research "sabotage" complaints : Several users report that Claude models quietly corrupt research workflows. Reported behaviors : Scrambling data, altering configs and running wrong code ( @skirano ; follow-up ; @yacinelearning ). Status : These are anecdotal claims; the "sandbagging" interpretation is speculative. GPT-6.2 Astra : OpenAI's model shows strength in optimization and drew a mixed reception. Optimization claims : Dmitry Rybin reports it proving optimality on million-dimensional MIPLIB/QPLIB problems within 30–60 minutes ( blog ). Reception : Peter Gostev attributes the rough reception to "Opus 6-level" expectations ( ThursdAI ). Persistence : Others note low persistence ( @ivan_bezdomny ). MAI-Code-2.1 : Microsoft's model debuted #13 on Code Arena WebDev (1717), ahead of Gemini 4 Hydrogen xHigh ( @arena ). Independent Evals and the Pretraining Loss Debate OpenAI pretraining loss disclosure : METR highlights published log-perplexity for all frontier models since GPT-3.5. Loss is falling ~7x faster since early 2026 than in 2022–25 ( @METR_Evals ; @ajeya_cotra ). Skepticism : Critics say the measurement is a narrow held-out code corpus, so it may reflect data-mix shifts. They cite OpenAI's own footnotes ( @NickEMoran ; @scaling01 ). Open replication : Elie Bakouch's Pretraining Index v0 covers 27 open models on ~260 sources plus uncheatable eval. Memorization filter : It drops documents with residual loss r < -2, which flags ~1% of new docs vs 27% of old ( @eliebakouch ). AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 : LLMs control a simulated Unitree G1 across 10 tasks ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Scores : GPT-6.2 Astra leads at 71.0, ahead of Fable 5.2 (57.5) and GPT-6.2 Sol (53.7). Failure points : Only five dishes reached the rack in 90 episodes. Seven of nine models broke a dish they had been told was fragile. FrontierPhysics : The benchmark has 54 private physicist-written research tasks ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Scores : Fable 5.2 leads at 32%, ahead of Astra at 26%. Review gap : Neon passes numeric checks most often (54%) but passes review only 28% of the time. Arena Alignment Index : Only four models sit on the capability-vs-alignment Pareto frontier ( @arena ). Leaders : GPT-6.2 Sol, GPT-6.2 Astra, GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.2. Sol has the top alignment score (85.5); Fable has the top capability score (1448). Spread : Similarly capable open models range from 81 to 52 on alignment. CyberOffense : Mistral Large 4 scored 37.0%, ranking #6 ( @ValsAI ). Search APIs : Octen returns results in ~0.17s and scores 82 on the AA Search Index ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Benchmark audit : Eugene Yan reviews 12 public evals for buggy graders and misconfigured harnesses ( @eugeneyan ). Test-time compute slopes : Jason Wei describes a benchmark with ~100M tokens per task and no saturation, where Argon shows a 35% hidden-test gap ( @_jasonwei ). Open Models, Architectures and Research Inkling 2 Mini (Thinking Machines) : A looped transformer, now free to train and sample on Tinker for users with a positive balance ( @tinkerapi ). Model ID : thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini:peft:65536:free ( details ). Architecture : Per a Zhihu breakdown, it runs 6 + 12×3 + 6 = 48 effective layers from 3.4B unique active parameters. Cache : The sliding-window design keeps the BF16 cache at ~4.2 GiB for 128K context.

item.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
item.abstract:
Back to Articles Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 2 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding. Results Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate. Config (1× RTX PRO 6000) 1-user decode (tok/s) 8-user aggregate (tok/s) Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s) TTFT SGLang, no speculation (baseline) 134–139 543–598 18.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K 41–114 ms vLLM, no speculation 157.0 638 20.7K / 20.7K 33 ms SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts) 166.6 — ¹ 18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K 38–51 ms vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts) 190.6 716 20.7K / 20.6K 40 ms Deployed endpoint (over the internet) 194.9 673 11.7K / 19.2K ² 198 ms ² ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM.
² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip. All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --tool-call-parser inkling \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser inkling \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work ). Why it stops around 190 tok/s Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job ( 1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s . Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits. Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s . At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth , so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer. What didn't work Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower: vLLM Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1). draft_sample_method: "greedy" −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s). rejection_sample_method: "block" 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect. enable_adaptive_verification Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter. draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8" Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters.

item.title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling
item.abstract:
Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models , where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block. However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs. Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute. This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer. Reactor , a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post. Improving throughput with NVFP4 NVIDIA RTX Blackwell has lower BF16 matmul throughput compared to the data center variants. While data center workloads are bounded by softmax (FlashAttention4 tries to solve this through pipelining and exp2 emulation), the NVIDIA RTX Blackwell is bounded by MMA on BF16 Attention. Due to higher TFLOP/s for NVFP4, throughput can be improved to achieve better performance. Attention compute The general attention computation and the two core matrix multiplications it involves are: Query-Key matrix multiplication (\(QK\)) : The first matmul in attention, \(QKᵀ\), where \(Q\) contains query vectors and \(K\) contains key vectors. It computes the attention scores used by softmax. Attention-Weight Value matrix multiplication (\(PV\)) : The second matmul in attention, \(PV\), where \(P\) contains softmax-derived attention weights and \(V\) contains value vectors. It combines the value vectors according to their attention weights to produce the output. In the tiled attention kernel discussed here, \(P\) contains unnormalized softmax weights, and final normalization is applied after the output has been accumulated across tiles (similar to FlashAttention). How SageAttention3 accelerates attention using NVFP4 SageAttention3 is a native NVFP4 attention mechanism specifically designed for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell streaming multiprocessor (SM) 120. It performs both \(QK\) and \(PV\) using NVFP4​. Its primary innovation came from performing two-level scaling for \(P\).​ NVFP4 quantization generates two tensors: an NVFP4 data tensor and an FP8 scaling tensor. Because ​softmax outputs are bound to a narrow [0, 1] range, they can underutilize the NVFP4 dynamic range, resulting in accuracy degradation. Two-level scaling addresses this by first normalizing the values to fully utilize dynamic range before quantizing the result. SageAttention3 cooperative thread array stable state design The SageAttention3 cooperative thread array (CTA) design is as follows: The CTA uses four producer warps and eight consumer warps. For each N128 tile, consumers execute \(QK\), softmax and probability quantization, and \(PV\) in sequence. While consumers perform softmax, scaling, and quantization, tensor-core activity has gaps. Video 1 illustrates this sequential execution. # Current SageAttention 3 CTA Execution (per N tile)
# CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer) For each N tile: # 1. Producer Role: Data Loading # Q is loaded once per M tile AsyncLoad(Q) # K, V, Scale Factors, and delta_s use 3-stage async TMA pipeline AsyncLoad(K, V, Scale_Factors, delta_s) # 2. Consumer Role: Dependency Chain (Serial Execution) # 8 Consumer warps (256-thread MMA collective) # A. QK Computation Execute_QK_OMMA() Apply_delta_s_correction() # B. Softmax & Quantization Apply_Masking() Execute_Online_Softmax() Execute_NVFP4_Probability_Quantization() # C. PV Computation Execute_PV_OMMA() # Note: Execution is strictly serial per N tile # No overlapping or independent fragments in flight The following observations can be drawn from this CTA design and the parallel thread execution (PTX) and instruction set architecture (ISA) for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs: First, TMA Loads are bound to Shapes of 128×128, not utilizing the entire shape would mean underutilizing our GPU bandwidth. Second, the NVIDIA Blackwell RTX OMMA operation remains constrained to m16, n8, k64 (where m and n represent LHS/RHS free dimensions, while k is the contraction axis), as specified by the PTX instruction mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X.m16n8k64 .​ To cover the full contraction dimension of k=128, two MMA instructions with k=64 must be issued. The current CTA design issues these instructions for \(QK\) in succession. Because MMA execution is synchronous, the issuing consumer warps wait for completion before proceeding to online softmax and intermediate quantization. This means that the operations within the stable loop are sequentially pipelined. There is a large gap in MMA activity, as there is no compute scheduled on the tensor cores. The warps are busy computing the softmax, scaling, and quantization operations. Video 1 shows the attention-kernel timeline, including sequential \(QK\) matrix multiplication, softmax, and \(PV\) matrix multiplication. Video 1. CTA timeline for original CTA design of SageAttention3 Register constraints Producer warps use 3,072 registers, and consumer warps use 59,392 registers. The total of 62,464 registers occupies approximately 95.3% of the SM’s register capacity. This leaves little room to hold an additional score tile while processing the current tile. Optimized CTA design The design retains four producer warps, eight consumer warps, and complete N128 K/V tile loads. The change is in how consumers compute and store attention scores. Each N128 score tile is split into two N64 halves, and each occupies a separate register slot. After one half has been exponentiated and quantized, its score registers are reused to compute the corresponding \(QK\) half of the next tile. This interleaves the next tile’s \(QK\) to work with the current tile’s remaining softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) operations. The online-softmax state is still updated across the complete N128 score tile before either half is consumed. Video 2 shows how this schedule fills gaps in tensor-core activity without allocating a second complete score tile. Video 2. CTA Timeline for optimized SageAttention3 The following pseudocode illustrates the optimized schedule, including the initial score computation, steady-state register reuse, and processing of the final tile. Unlike the original design, which completes \(QK\), softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) sequentially for each N128 tile, the optimized design splits the score tile into two N64 register slots. When half is quantized, its score registers are reused for the next tile’s \(QK\) computation.

item.title: [AINews] Gemini 4 Neon marks GDM's full return as a Frontier Lab
item.abstract: Three months ago, shortly after the Demis/Dean/etc departures , and with disappointing progress on Gemini 3 models, people had publicly given up on Google DeepMind as a frontier lab. Today, apologies are being issued , and Neon is the talk of the town! Despite giving Gemini 4 Argon (RIP), Carbon and Neon the title story (with Hydrogen a near miss ), we are exercising yet another rare double-feature choice to highlight the unusually strong breakout trend in Neon’s adoption: If this seems like a coordinated hype campaign, it very probably isn’t, mostly because the names we feature can’t be bought, especially coming up to the end. AI News for 11/23/2026-11/24/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Frontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel Bugs VP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs : An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field ( @kimmonismus , repo pointer ). OpenAI's counter-release : OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement ( @AndrewCurran_ ). Scope : The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds ( @ZhihuFrontier ). Speculation : Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion. Riemann proof clarifications : Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" ( @kimmonismus , @simonw ). Lineage claim : A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference ( @ZhihuFrontier ). GPT-6 protein design, wet-lab validated : OpenAI released a preprint showing GPT-6 models designing new protein shapes and sequences through reasoning and code, without specialized bio models ( @OpenAI ). Results : 14 of 107 resequenced proteins showed binding. 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 antibody fragments retained binding ( details ). Cost caveat : On a prior DNA task, GPT-6.1 Sol was about 2,000x more expensive per task than a specialized model ( @_lewtun ). GPT-6 Cyber and the Linux kernel : In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root and generated patches for maintainer review ( @OpenAI ). Discovery beyond verifiable domains : A historian says GPT-6.2 Astra identified the vicomte de Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes. It also surfaced an obscure microfilmed diary whose handwriting and itinerary matched the sketches ( @HistoryGPT ). Exoplanet candidates : Amateurs using Codex and Astra searched Kepler and TESS data. One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged ( @OpenAI ). Robotics saturation : GPT-6.2 Astra on Codex scored 97% on RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 across 120 real-robot trials, and RoboDojo is being retired ( @robocurve ). New environments : Einsia released RoboUniverse-10K, a set of 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim tasks built from real manipulation videos. The top frontier score on held-out tasks is 85.8%, while 7 of 11 models score ≤10% ( @EinsiaAI ). Gemini 4 Neon Rollout and Frontier Model Moves Gemini 4 Neon adoption : Neon set a Day-1 usage record on Google's paid APIs. Antigravity tokens/day are up 82% since Argon launched six weeks ago ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Neon is now available to Google Workspace customers through the Gemini app ( @OfficialLoganK ). Third-party volume : Perplexity has passed 120B Neon tokens, doubling daily volume in 3 days with 36B on Monday. Arav Srinivas places Neon "between Opus and Fable" in intelligence but best on response style ( @AravSrinivas ). Developer tooling : Google shipped an experimental anti-slop frontend-design skill for Neon ( @_philschmid ) and made eight Workspace MCP servers plus gwscli generally available, with 5,000 requests/day free per product ( @_philschmid ). Price-performance (attributed estimate) : One estimate puts Neon xhigh roughly equal to Opus Max, at $6.44 vs $10.04 per Artificial Analysis task ( @teortaxesTex ). Sycophancy concerns : Several users report heavy "glazing" and overcorrection when Neon is critiqued ( @teortaxesTex , @johnowhitaker ). Claude Opus 5.6 sightings (unconfirmed) : Users report Opus 5.6 being A/B-tested in Claude Code and chat, and describe it as "quite a jump" over 5.5 ( @synthwavedd , @kimmonismus ). Cognition SWE-2.1 : The model is pure-RL trained on Kimi K3 and reportedly approaches frontier models on FrontierCode 2.0 at max reasoning. It is free on Devin paid tiers for two weeks ( @cognition ). Looped transformers trend : GLM-5.4 makes five looped models in Raschka's architecture gallery ( @rasbt ). SenseNova-Loop-9B : The model runs its middle 24 of 32 layers twice and beats Qwen3.8-27B on GAIA (69.90 vs 66.99). It is about 4.9 GB at 4-bit and released under Apache 2.0 ( @kimmonismus ). Inkling 2 Mini decoding : LoopCD contrasts loop pass 3 against pass 1 with no training, lifting AA-Omniscience from -9.0 to -3.4 ( @onloglogn ). Inkling 2 Mini evals : Reported scores include #1 under 32B on DeepSWE (48.2%) and 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified ( @victormustar ). Fine-tuning speedups : Unsloth fine-tuning of the model is up to 3x faster with 50% less VRAM ( @danielhanchen ). ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview : A 280B/14B-active MoE with up to 1M context, served in vLLM with a DSpark draft model averaging more than 4 accepted tokens ( @vllm_project ). Ling-3.2-air : A 124B/5.5B-active multimodal MoE ( @vllm_project ). OCR models : LlamaIndex released OCRia-1 (4B, Qwen-based) and OCRia-nano-1 (8.1M parameters, about 426 ms/page on one CPU core) under a modified RAIL-M license requiring a commercial license above $2M in revenue or funding ( @jerryjliu0 , license detail ). Datalab's Indra OCR 1.2, Apache 2.0, uses a roughly 1M-parameter CTC recognizer at 50 ms/page on 32 cores ( @VikParuchuri ). Evals and Measurement Disputes Harness Comparisons (Artificial Analysis) : The same model varies sharply by harness ( @ArtificialAnlys ). No universal best harness : GPT-6 Luna scores best in Codex (26), where GLM-5.3-Flash ranks last. GLM scores best in Claude Code (39). Cost spread : Cost varies more than score, from $0.11 to $0.62 per task for Luna. Behavior change : GLM reasons in terse fragments inside Codex, producing 52k output tokens vs 97–202k elsewhere. Perplexity as a shared intelligence metric : Following Jakub Pachocki's "Perplexity and Intelligence," Mercor proposes a proxy averaging six multiple-choice benchmarks at minimal reasoning. They report strong correlation with OpenAI's numbers at $37 for a full GPT-6.2 Astra run ( @_jasonwei ). Interpretation : Giffman reads the debate as being about evaluating base models, not imposing an exact standard ( @giffmana ). Validity question : Ethan Perez asks whether the correlation holds across labs ( @EthanJPerez ). Humanity's First Exam (DeepMind/Kaggle) : The benchmark measures "floor reliability" with 544 prompts in 136 families ( @kaggle ). Results : Top models hit 96–98% pass@1 but average 85.6% on family pass^4. Visual perception drives 74% of errors. Leaderboard : GPT-6.2 Astra leads at 90.7%, followed by Sol and Neon. Agent Arena Index : Fable 5.2 leads by 134 points ( @arena ). 3D leaderboard : Fable 5.2 leads with 1933 points, and 3D battles produce fewer ties (8% vs 13%) ( @arena ).

item.title: 華人計算機視覺泰斗二次創業！離開蘋果下場，專注下一代空間與物理AI
item.abstract: 華人計算機視覺泰斗二次創業！離開蘋果下場，專注下一代空間與物理AI 衡宇 2026-11-25 14:49:27 來源： 量子位 複雜場景三維建模成本降至10美元以內 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 蘋果空間智慧首席科學家告別蘋果，殺入空間與物理AI賽道創業。 “單純的3D建模生成，可能逐漸被大語言模型吞掉。”作為視覺幾何的世界級奠基者，看到今年9月釋出的GPT-6-Astra所展現出的空間理解和三維重建能力，研究三維視覺近40年的 權龍 很難無動於衷。 1988年，他發表ICCV華人計算機視覺第一篇論文；1995年提出奠定三檢視重建基礎的“六點演算法”；後來成為香港科技大學視覺研究第一人，培養出一批活躍在中國計算機視覺領域的學者和創業者。 2015年，權龍創辦三維重建雲平臺Altizure，公司於2020年被蘋果收購，他本人也隨之加入蘋果、出任蘋果空間智慧首席科學家。 現在，權龍帶著新公司 格秩科技 （Envision AI） 重新下場，從最擅長的三維視覺出發，去構建原生的空間與物理AI基礎模型 （Spatial&Physical AI） 。 “Envision AI希望補足當前大語言模型在表達空間、物理資訊以及泛化能力上的缺陷。”權龍表示。 這種“反其道而行之”的底層架構，已經展現出驚人的效率差距。 在大規模空間 （如城市） 三維建模這類極度複雜的任務上，GPT-6-Astra往往需要數小時才能完成推理，單場景成本高達100至600美元；而Envision AI自研的原生基座模型 ，單場景推理成本壓低至不到10美元。 不僅算力與Token開銷大幅降低，其場景規模與精細程度也優於主流大模型，整體構建效率實現了一個數量級的提升。 △ 上述影片不是實拍結果，而是直接輸出的3D場景渲染結果 而在被視為物理AI最大攔路虎之一的資料層方面，這家剛剛官宣的初創公司已建立起包含3000萬高質量空間物理資料資產、4000萬+空間物理影片資料，以及500萬+複雜場景的龐大護城河。 3D視覺泰斗拉起一支創業精銳之師 從經典視覺幾何到深度學習，再到如今的空間智慧與物理AI， 權龍近四十年的科研生涯，幾乎貫穿了現代計算機視覺的整部演進史。 1980年代，權龍作為改革開放後首批公派留學生赴法深造，在法國國立洛林理工學院攻讀博士，隨後加入法國國家資訊與自動化研究所 （INRIA） ，師從法國射影幾何與計算機視覺先驅Roger Mohr。 1988年，權龍在計算機視覺頂會ICCV上發表了歷史上第一篇由華人學者撰寫的論文。 20世紀90年代，歐洲正處於三維計算機視覺研究的黃金年代。法國INRIA、牛津大學等機構聚集了一批研究多檢視幾何、三維重建的頂尖學者。 1995年，權龍提出著名的“六點演算法” ，徹底解決了三檢視幾何的經典難題並一戰成名，奠定了其在三維重建領域的國際領軍地位。 彼時在法國求學和從事研究的三位華人學者——權龍、馬頌德 （中科院自動化所研究員、博導） 、張正友 （騰訊首席科學家、Robotics X實驗室主任） ，後來深刻推動了國內計算機視覺領域的起步，在業內被稱作 “法國華人視覺三劍客” 。 △ 權龍、馬頌德、張正友，圖片由AI生成 2001年，權龍回國加入香港科技大學， 一手創立了VisGraph （Vision + Graphics） 實驗室，成為港科大視覺研究第一人。 在此後二十餘年間，他培養出港科大教授譚平、百度計算機視覺首席科學家王井東、AutoX創始人肖健雄、曠視前上海研究院院長危夷晨、北大智慧學院/資訊科學中心研究員/博導曾鋼、微軟亞洲研究院首席研究經理袁路等一眾國內CV學術界與產業界人才。 目前，權龍的谷歌學術被引用數超2.3萬次。 權龍不是一位只呆在象牙塔裡的學者。 十年前，他就開始嘗試將三維視覺技術推向真實產品。 2015年，消費級無人機和智慧手機快速普及，攝像頭開始以前所未有的規模記錄現實世界。 抓住這個時間點，權龍與自己的博士生方天、姚遙等人在2015年共同創立了三維重建雲平臺Altizure。 利用Altizure，使用者只需要通過無人機、手機等裝置拍攝照片，就能將現實場景重建為三維模型。 後來，Altizure逐漸轉向智慧城市、測繪和地理資訊等企業級市場。 △ 圖片由AI生成 憑藉在端側三維重建上的驚豔表現，Altizure在2020年被蘋果收購。蘋果甚至專門為此在香港中環設立研發中心並擴大招人。 被收購後，權龍出任蘋果空間智慧首席科學家。 在蘋果內部，權龍團隊繼續深耕端側三維重建與空間智慧，參與了ARKit、Apple Vision Pro、Apple Intelligence以及Object Capture API等產品和技術的研發，為蘋果的空間感知、三維重建能力提供演算法支援。 對於權龍而言， 這段經歷意味著他苦心鑽研多年的三維視覺演算法，進入了面向海量使用者的消費電子產品。 但隨著ChatGPT引發新一輪AI技術變革，本可以在蘋果“躺平養老”的他，又開始坐不住了。 對技術視窗具有敏銳嗅覺的權龍，有著一份“不想被時代甩開”的緊迫感。 在幾乎完整經歷了計算機視覺此前數十年發展的他看來，這一輪生成式AI與空間物理智慧的技術路線正在迅速收斂，“我在三維視覺幹了快四十年，這時候不下場，很可能就被行業甩開了，再往後剩下的時間，就真只能養老、打網球了。” 於是，權龍開始認真考慮離開蘋果再次創業。 有了再次創業的念頭後，權龍開始著手組建一支全新的團隊。 這一次，他希望從底層架構入手，探索空間與物理AI的統一基礎模型。相比過去專注於三維重建的技術研發，新目標需要同時打通視覺、幾何、物理與大模型推理能力，對團隊的研究背景和工程能力也提出了不同要求。 他說： 適應上一代產品研發模式的工程師未必適合大模型時代，做基座模型需要思路切換極快、真正屬於AI Native時代的年輕人。 圍繞空間物理基座模型，權龍集結了一支橫跨兩代師承、兼具學術研究與大廠工程經驗的聯創班底—— 作為創始人、董事長，權龍本人主要負責技術戰略、整體架構方向和人才培養。 聯合創始人兼CEO張飛虎 博士畢業於牛津大學電腦科學系，是最早將深度學習引入3D視覺、開展Sim2Real研究的青年學者之一，研究曾入圍CVPR最佳論文最終候選名單，谷歌學術引用超4000次。 Envision AI已是他的第三段創業經歷。 此前，張飛虎曾參與創立後來被谷歌收購的6d.ai，隨後創辦DreamTech，推出全球首個公開的原生3D大模型Direct3D，相關工作被Meta、蘋果、Adobe等科技巨頭引用。 DreamTech時期，張飛虎團隊率先提出端到端3D Diffusion Transformer架構，推動3D生成邁向Scaling Law時代。 Direct3D背後還有一位研究者，如今同樣位列Envision AI的創始團隊—— 姚遙，公司聯合創始人兼前沿探索負責人 。 他博士畢業於權龍門下，曾是Altizure時的創始成員，後隨收購進入蘋果任高階研究員，現任南京大學副教授。 姚遙谷歌學術被引量破萬，其代表作涵蓋開創深度學習三維重建的MVSNet、Direct3D及Agentic 3D系列。 在今年格外引發關注的螞蟻靈波 （LingBot） 系列模型中，他也曾參與小時級開源互動世界模型LingBot-World 2.0和流式3D重建基礎模型LingBot-Map兩項工作，是LingBot-Map的共同通訊作者。 迄今為止，LingBot-Map在GitHub攬星19.1k，還獲得ECCV 2026最佳論文提名。 聯合創始人兼工程負責人許景禧 的代表作，則是一款大眾熟悉的軟體——騰訊會議。 許景禧是香港中文大學計算機博士，師從IEEE Computer Society首位華人主席華雲生，是其關門弟子。 作為騰訊會議初創團隊成員及影片傳輸演算法負責人，他深度參與了騰訊會議、企業微信會議從0到1的研發，相關產品曾獲得騰訊最高獎。 在Envision AI，許景禧負責AI基礎設施、工程架構與大規模系統部署。 創始團隊中還有另一位從經典視覺幾何時代一路走來的學者。 聯合創始人兼首席科學家Philip Torr 是牛津大學工程科學終身教授、英國皇家學會及皇家工程院雙院士，也是張飛虎的博士導師。 早在1998年，他便憑藉三維視覺研究獲得計算機視覺領域最高獎項之一的“馬爾獎”。 △ 圖片由AI生成 在這套核心管理層之下，Envision AI的研發團隊清一色由90後骨幹與00後極客組成。 成立時間不長的Envision AI，已吸納數十位來自海內外高校的00後博士生。這支年輕團隊試圖以更精簡的組織規模，聚集接近頭部大廠研究團隊的人才配置。 大模型開始吞噬3D，空間物理AI還有什麼機會？ 今年9月，OpenAI釋出的GPT-6-Astra給整個具身智慧與3D賽道敲響了警鐘。 過去需要依靠專用模型完成的部分空間理解、物理推理與動作規劃任務，如今已經進入通用大模型的能力範圍。 在權龍看來，這一變化正在重新定義空間與物理AI領域的競爭規則。 首先，大模型的泛化能力，正在直接兼併垂直的具身模型與世界模型。 在輝達RoboLab-120模擬基準測試中，GPT-6-Astra通過任務分解、空間記憶與工具呼叫等Agent工作流程，取得了74.8%的操作成功率。 △ 圖片由AI生成 其次，傳統3D視覺公司的天花板已經顯現。 目前市場上基於3D DiT架構的3D生成公司，核心解決的是“形狀和外觀像不像”的問題，輸出的是靜態的視覺資產。 這一技術路線相對應的是缺乏對底層物理規律、材質屬性和空間邏輯的表達，很難往下走到物理互動那一層。 最後，主流大模型的“外掛式”路徑存在天然的效率瓶頸。 像GPT-6-Astra這類從純語言基模演進出的多模態路線，本質上仍是以語言為骨幹，靠呼叫Agent和外部CAD工具去理解與重建物理世界。 這種互動方式流程複雜，推理效率極低，算力開銷還是天文數字，很難滿足物理世界即時互動的嚴苛要求。 正如開頭所提到的，拿一張圖讓GPT-6-Astra建個模，動輒需要等上好幾個小時。 時間、token、真金白銀，都像水一樣嘩嘩流走了。 權龍認為，隨著空間與物理任務越來越複雜，完全依賴龐大的語言模型來處理這些問題，未必是最高效的選擇。 那麼，空間與物理AI真正的機會到底在哪？ “未來物理AI的競爭焦點，將從單一任務的專用小模型， 轉向能夠同時處理多種空間與物理任務的統一基礎模型 。”權龍判斷。 在權龍看來，下一代空間與物理AI的突破口需要從更底層的模型架構中尋找。 也因此，Envision AI選擇 打造原生的空間與物理統一基座模型。 團隊希望延續大語言模型已有的推理、規劃與泛化能力，同時從三維幾何與物理規律出發，探索更適合表達真實世界的底層表徵與計算架構。 最終要攻克的，是空間與物理AI的泛化難題，讓模型習得的空間與物理知識能夠跨任務、跨場景遷移，降低對特定任務訓練和外部工具的依賴。 △ 圖片由AI生成 從三維重建到理解物理世界，Envision AI準備怎麼做？ 具體怎麼做？ Envision AI將下一代空間物理AI需要解決的問題，概括為三個遞進的層次： 空間——物理——泛化。 第一步是理解空間。 傳統大模型的位置編碼 （Positional Encoding） 主要用於表達序列中的位置資訊，而真正的空間智慧，需要顯式處理物體的三維位置、形狀、尺度以及複雜的幾何拓撲關係。 第二步是理解物理。 在掌握空間結構的基礎上，進一步表達物體的材質、運動、受力、光照反射以及隨時間變化的物理因果關係，讓機器既能描述世界現在的狀態，也能預判施加某個動作後可能發生的變化。 第三步是實現泛化。 通過大規模混合訓練，讓模型掌握的空間與物理知識能夠遷移到此前未見過的任務和場景中。 要在同一個基礎模型中實現這些能力，首先需要解決不同模態的資訊表達問題。 在模型架構打破“語言基模打補丁”的常規路徑的基礎上，Envision AI的技術思路是空間與物理的形式化 （Formalization） 。 自然語言是離散的，而影像與物理空間具有連續、高維等特性。 權龍認為，自然語言 （Natural Language） 只是語言的一部分，科學系統中的數學語言、計算機中的程式語言 （Programming Language） ，同樣能夠承擔資訊表達與邏輯推理的任務。 團隊正在探索將空間位置、幾何結構、局部編輯規則、光影渲染乃至物理場邏輯納入統一的形式化表徵體系，讓複雜的物理世界能夠以機器可推理、可解釋、可編輯的方式得到表達。 按照Envision item.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
item.abstract: Back to Articles An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 7 +1 Vrunda Gadesha vrunda-gadesha Follow ibm-research Cyril Shaji cyrilshaji Follow ibm-research Jobit Treesa Varughese jotreesa1 Follow ibm-research Nivetha Suruliraj nivetha-suruliraj Follow ibm-research Anu Sugunan anu24-hugface Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Jaydeep Sen JaydeepSen Follow ibm-research Amith Singhee asinghee Follow ibm-research Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps . The use case: a Farm Assistant A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: Listens and turns the speech into text. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked. If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. Where CUGA fits CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() . Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's. The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. The hard part is not the voice Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages. Making it sound right and keeping it safe A few small decisions mattered more than we expected: Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast. Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user. Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key. Try it You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer: CUGA Apps on Hugging Face → Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn. Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust. This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity. If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core . Learn more about CUGA New to CUGA? Here are some places to start: cuga.dev : the CUGA home page. CUGA on GitHub : the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue. CUGA documentation : setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration. CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub : the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space. Spaces you can try in your browser: CUGA Agent : the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario. CUGA Apps : launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard. CUGA Policy Playground : two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without. More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog: CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents : the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes. Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness : the app gallery this voice agent belongs to. item.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
item.abstract: Back to Articles Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. Helping researchers check the work For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Keep scientific judgment in the loop Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation. Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said. Context mattered, too.

item.title: Why Linear says Issue Tracking is Dead — Cristina Cordova, COO
item.abstract: Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion → Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently. Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. Jump to the sales team discussion → Everyone wants outcome-based pricing Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't? item.title: The Roadmap to Becoming an AI Security Engineer in 2027
item.abstract: The Roadmap to Becoming an AI Security Engineer in 2027 From cybersecurity foundations to defending machine learning systems, agentic pipelines, and large language model applications. By Vinod Chugani on November 25, 2026 in Career Advice The attack surface has changed. Organizations building AI-powered products need security engineers who understand what's actually new here: model theft, training data poisoning, inference attacks, privacy risks from embedding memorization, and the governance requirements that come with deploying these systems at scale. This created a role that simply didn't exist five years ago. An AI security engineer protects machine learning systems from attacks targeting their data, models, and infrastructure, which involves working across the full lifecycle of an AI product rather than focusing on traditional network perimeters or web application layers. The market reflects that shift. In one analysis, 28.5% of cybersecurity job postings between October 2025 and March 2026 required AI skills, up from 14.2% in the same period a year earlier. ZipRecruiter puts the average US AI security engineer salary at \$152,773 per year as of August 2026, with the top 10% near \$205,000. This roadmap covers six steps to get there, starting from prerequisites and moving into specialized practice areas that hiring teams are actively looking for right now. Step 1: Building Core Security and Programming Foundations There's no shortcut past this step. AI security engineering is a specialization built on top of general security knowledge, so the foundation has to be solid before you can layer AI-specific skills on top. On the security side, focus on networking fundamentals (TCP/IP, DNS, TLS), operating system internals, authentication and access control, and application security concepts like injection vulnerabilities, insecure deserialization, and broken authorization. These translate directly into AI security work. Many large language model (LLM) and machine learning vulnerabilities are extensions of classic security problems. On the programming side, Python is non-negotiable. Python, secure coding, API hardening, cloud-native security, and familiarity with machine learning frameworks show up consistently across job descriptions in this field. Focus on writing Python you can actually audit: understand how your code handles untrusted inputs, where injection points live, and how secrets management works in modern applications. Learning objectives for this step: Complete a CompTIA Security+ certification or equivalent to establish a shared vocabulary with hiring managers Build a working knowledge of the OWASP Top 10 and how each vulnerability class appears in web and API contexts Write at least five Python scripts that interact with APIs, handle authentication, and process data inputs with validation Resources: TryHackMe , Hack The Box , the OWASP Testing Guide , and Python's official documentation (pay particular attention to the subprocess , hashlib , and secrets modules). Step 2: Understanding How Machine Learning Systems Work You can't defend systems you don't understand. Before getting into adversarial machine learning or LLM security, you need a solid mental model of how these systems are built and where they're structurally fragile. This step doesn't require a PhD in machine learning. What you need is enough depth to understand what a training pipeline looks like, how a model ingests and memorizes data, what inference means in a production context, and how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures retrieve and inject external content at runtime. Pay close attention to how LLMs differ from classical machine learning models in terms of their attack surface. LLMs process natural language as input, which means the boundary between "instruction" and "data" is blurry by design. That blurriness is exactly where prompt injection comes from, one of the defining vulnerability classes of this role. Learning objectives for this step: Complete a machine learning fundamentals course focused on supervised learning, model training, and evaluation Build a simple RAG application using an open-source LLM to understand retrieval pipelines and embedding storage Document the data flow in your RAG build: where does untrusted content enter, and what can it influence? Resources: fast.ai Practical Deep Learning , LangChain documentation , and Hugging Face Transformers for hands-on model work. from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings # docs: a list of LangChain Document objects loaded earlier (e.g. with a document loader) # Load and embed documents into a vector store embedding = OpenAIEmbeddings() vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(docs, embedding) retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever() This setup is exactly where untrusted documents can inject content. Analyzing this retrieval step is a core AI security engineering task. Step 3: Learning the AI-Specific Threat Model AI security engineering is adversarial and technical: you build controls and you try to break them. Step 3 is where you start thinking like an attacker (specifically against AI systems). The core threat categories to study: Prompt injection : Direct and indirect prompt injection, where malicious content in retrieved documents or user input overrides system instructions. Think of it as the SQL injection of the LLM era. Training data poisoning : Manipulating the data a model learns from to influence its outputs in a targeted way. This matters most for models that ingest user-generated content. Model extraction and theft : Using a series of queries to reconstruct a proprietary model's behavior or steal its capabilities. This is a real commercial and intellectual property risk for organizations deploying fine-tuned models. Adversarial inputs : Inputs crafted to cause a model to misclassify or behave in unintended ways. This is most relevant for image classifiers and content moderation systems. Data leakage through memorization : LLMs can memorize and reproduce training data verbatim, including sensitive personal or proprietary information, sometimes without any obvious trigger. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is the most structured reference for this threat landscape and should be your primary study document at this stage. Work through each category, understand the attack mechanics, and think about how you'd detect or prevent each one. Step 4: Developing Hands-On Red Teaming and Defense Skills The skills that made a good Security Operations Center (SOC) analyst (adversarial thinking, operational context, pattern recognition, understanding of attacker behavior) are exactly what make a good AI security engineer. This step puts that thinking into practice against actual AI systems. Red teaming AI systems means systematically probing them for vulnerabilities using structured methods. At a minimum, practice these: Running prompt injection attacks against LLM applications, including indirect injection through RAG pipelines Testing content filters for bypass techniques using encoding, language switching, and role-play framing Evaluating guardrail robustness by attempting to elicit restricted outputs through multi-turn conversation On the defensive side, learn how to implement the controls that counter these attacks. Output filtering, input sanitization, privilege separation for agentic systems, and rate limiting are the basics. More advanced controls include sandboxing tool calls in agentic pipelines, implementing LLM firewalls, and designing least-privilege access patterns for models that interact with external APIs. # Simple output filter to detect potential data leakage def check_output(response: str, sensitive_patterns: list) -> bool: for pattern in sensitive_patterns: if pattern.lower() in response.lower(): return False # Flag for review return True This kind of lightweight guardrail is a starting point.

item.title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
item.abstract: AI Tech Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths? Companies like Akai have decided to embrace the modding community rather than resist vibe coders. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 25, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Image: The Verge; Adobe Stock Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world , leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source. The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic , the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge . That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key . Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.” Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick , a clone of the E-mu SP-1200 , the Anima DJ controller , the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch. M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The company also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well. Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine , but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge . “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.” “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community.” While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he says, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.” Polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish company’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets users vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension. Elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.” Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the company has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced . Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the company, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.” Other major music manufacturers, like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation – all of whom did not comment for this story – have yet to issue any public statements about the explosion of AI-aided custom firmwares. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Terrence O'Brien AI Tech

item.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
item.abstract: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”
